title: Investment companies: how to analyze holding companies
description: Investment companies: why P/E misleads, how net asset value is calculated and the P/B ladder 0.60–3.13 in the universe's four companies.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
# Investment companies: how to analyze investment companies

**Investment companies own shares in other companies instead of running an operation of their own.** The accounts therefore mirror the value of the holdings, and metrics such as P/E and margins become almost meaningless. [AK1A's company universe](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026) contains four of the exchange's heaviest family members: Industrivärden, Investor, Latour and Kinnevik. Their numbers show the entire span — from a 40 percent discount to book value to more than three times book value. Here is how the analysis is built, step by step.

## What are investment companies — the company that owns companies

An [investment company](/kurser/ib-01-vad-ar-ett-investmentbolag) is a listed company whose business idea is to own and develop shares in other companies. Operations are minimal: no factory, no stores, only a balance sheet full of shares. That creates two economic engines — the value development of the holdings and active ownership: board seats, strategy and capital when needed. The capital has no maturity, which [eternal capital](/kurser/ib-06-evighetskapitalet) explains: ownership can be carried through entire business cycles without forced selling at the bottom.

The mechanism behind the entire guide is that the share trades freely on the exchange. The price is set by what buyers and sellers are prepared to pay in each moment — not by a manager redeeming shares at net asset value, as in an open fund. The price can therefore land anywhere in relation to NAV — a gap the family's methodology exists to measure and understand.

For you as an analyst, the income statement becomes a mirror of the exchange. When holdings rise, unrealized value gains flow through earnings under IFRS; when the market falls, the losses make the same journey. Our [analysis of Investor](/blogg/analys-investor-2026) summarizes it: the metrics are not comparable with operating companies. That is the thread through the entire guide.

## Why a P/E of 3.7 does not mean cheap — the income statement as a mirror

Take Industrivärden. The universe's raw data (retrieved 2026-09-03) shows a gross margin of 100 percent, an EBIT margin of 99.9 percent and a net margin of 99.3 percent — numbers that would make any manufacturer look like a money machine. They are instead a photograph of the accounting form: almost no operating costs are set against the large value changes. A P/E of 3.7 should therefore not be read as cheap, but as a sign that earnings are driven by something other than sales. [The P/E course](/kurser/km-009-pe) builds on earnings recurring — here the profit is a stock market curve in disguise.

The volatility is just as striking. Industrivärden's operating result went from plus 26.6 billion kronor in 2021 to minus 14.0 billion in 2022 — a swing of more than 40 billion in one year, without the portfolio companies changing anywhere near that much. The effect on the multiple is equally misleading: divided by earnings that change sign between years, the P/E becomes a measure of chance — the same portfolio can show a low multiple one year and a negative or enormous one the next. The comparison belongs at NAV level, not in earnings. The lesson appears in our [read-through of Industrivärden's quarterly report](/blogg/sa-laser-du-industrivarden-q3-2026): earnings are the weather, NAV is the climate.

## Net asset value and NAV — pricing the share against the holdings

The core of the analysis is instead net asset value, often called NAV: the sum of the holdings' value minus debts, per share. Setting the share price against NAV gives exactly [the P/B ratio](/kurser/v05-pb) — [the book value guide](/blogg/pb-tal-nar-jamfor-man-bokvarde-ratt) walks through the calculation.

This is the calculation with Investor's numbers. The universe's raw data measures P/B 1.159 — a share price of 410.75 kronor against a net asset value of around 354 kronor per share, that is a premium of about 16 percent. During 2026 the net asset value has risen from 355 via 367 to 397 kronor, an increase of 11.8 percent: when NAV grows faster than the price, the premium eats itself. The same ratio applied to Kinnevik gives the opposite: P/B 0.598 means a 40.2 percent discount to book value. Between the extremes sits Industrivärden at 1.03 — in practice traded at level with NAV.

An important nuance is the quality of the net asset value, which [the quality-of-NAV course](/kurser/ib-02-substansens-kvalitet) sorts out: listed holdings are valued at the exchange's price in real time, unlisted ones at assumptions nobody can control. The larger the unlisted share, the greater the uncertainty — and often a larger discount as well. That gives a practical control question for every NAV figure: how much of it can you verify against real-time listings? A NAV carried predominantly by listed holdings can be checked continuously; one resting on assumptions about unlisted companies requires trust in the manager's valuations — and the more trust required, the higher the return demanded. Companies with many different parts can also be valued piece by piece with [the sum-of-the-parts method](/kurser/km-012-sum-of-the-parts-sotp).

## The geography of the discount — the P/B ladder 0.60 to 3.13

The universe's four companies form a ladder that summarizes the family's logic:

- **Kinnevik 0.60** — 40.2 percent below book value, after four straight loss years: minus 19.5, 4.8, 2.6 and 3.3 billion, altogether around 30.3 billion kronor. The discount is a price on uncertainty: the revaluation of the holdings was real, and the market prices the risk that it continues.
- **Industrivärden 1.03** — share price at level with NAV. [The analysis of Industrivärden](/blogg/analys-industrivarden-2026) also shows ROE of 32.3 percent — but that too is a mirror: the return is carried by the exchange's swings, not by stable operations.
- **Investor 1.16** — a premium of about 16 percent. [The Wallenberg sphere](/kurser/km-068-wallenbergsfaren) and the long ownership mean the market pays for governance and persistence — a study in [Mr. Market psychology](/blogg/mr-market-psykologi-svenska-borsen): sometimes the market pays for safety, sometimes it punishes the same thing.
- **Latour 3.13** — more than three times book value. The company consolidates its operating subsidiaries, so revenue grew from 22.6 to 28.1 billion kronor 2022–2025, around 7.6 percent per year, and its P/E of 20.5 is the family's only multiple that looks like an operating company's. The premium to book value is carried by unlisted holdings — a reminder that [the conglomerate discount](/kurser/vr-09-konglomeratrabatten) can also strike the other way.

The span is striking: 3.13 divided by 0.60 is more than five times, and the family's median is 1.09. Two companies, Kinnevik and Latour, trade on either side of 1.0 — a difference explained not by the multiple but by NAV quality, governance and earnings history. Hence the guide's most important warning: a discount is never in itself a sign of mispricing. Kinnevik's four loss years were real revaluations of the holdings, and the discount may as well be a reasonable pricing of uncertainty as an exaggerated fear premium. The analyst's job is to tell the two apart — not to hunt the family's lowest ratio. Compare with [the industry medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2): where operating companies are valued on profits, what is valued here is ownership.

## Checklist: five steps when you analyze investment companies

1. **NAV first.** Find net asset value per share and split it into listed and unlisted. Ask: how much of the value can you verify against the exchange?
2. **The discount against history.** Set P/B in relation to the company's own history and the family's median — 1.09 across the universe's four. A changed discount is a changed story, not necessarily a changed value.
3. **Read the balance sheet, not the income statement.** With P/E 3.7 and a gross margin of 100 percent, earnings are a mirror. [The balance sheet course](/kurser/bk-01-balansrakningen) and [the anatomy of the NAV discount](/blogg/begreppet-substansrabatt) provide the methodology.
4. **Judge the ownership.** Who owns, for how long and with what reputation? Governance can justify a premium — its absence can justify a discount.
5. **Count on costs and dividends.** The management fee eats NAV every year; the dividend policy ([equity and dividends](/kurser/km-005-eget-kapital-utdelningar)) decides how much of the value reaches you as an owner.

Five steps, one family and a single idea: in investment companies the balance sheet is the truth and the share price is an opinion about it. It is a practice ground for separating price from value — the foundation of fundamental analysis.

_Sources: AK1A's 262-company universe (Yahoo Finance/MarketStack, raw data 2026-09-03); [Investor AB](https://www.investorab.com); [AB Industrivärden](https://www.industrivarden.se); [Kinnevik](https://www.kinnevik.com); [Investment AB Latour](https://www.latour.se)._

_This is educational financial analysis, not investment advice._
